When a health agency says a study “found an association,” it doesn’t mean one thing caused the other — and that’s one of the trickiest parts of reading science news. Think about it this way: ice cream sales and sunburns both go up in summer, but ice cream doesn’t cause sunburn. Researchers work hard to untangle these kinds of links by adjusting for other factors, but they can’t always be sure. So when you read a headline, look for words like “may,” “linked to,” or “associated with.” Check how many people were studied, and whether the finding has been repeated. One study is a clue, not an answer. Good science is slow, and that’s a feature, not a bug.
